title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
What you’ll build
Follow this guide to build your first academic website:

a home page with your photo and a short bio
a research page
a teaching page
your CV

Your website will be at https://USERNAME.github.io. There’s no payment required unless you want a custom domain name (see the extension at the end).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
What you’ll build
USERNAME is a placeholder for your own GitHub username. My USERNAME is carlislerainey, so my repository is called carlislerainey.github.io and my site is at https://carlislerainey.github.io. Put your USERNAME wherever you see the placeholder.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Examples
These three are pretty close to what you’ll have after you finish this guide:

Artur Baranov, a PhD candidate at Northwestern, uses jolla, the centered layout we start from. Source is on GitHub.
Maranda Joyce, a PhD candidate at Rice, uses trestles and one of Quarto’s dark themes. Source is on GitHub.
Tyler Rongxuan Chen, a PhD candidate at Michigan, uses solana and almost the same row of buttons you will make. Source is on GitHub.

These two have a bit of customization.

Charlotte Kuberka, a PhD candidate at LSE, kept trestles and restyled it to match her CV. Source is on GitHub.
Frederik Hjorth, a professor at Copenhagen, has a page each for his papers, his teaching, and his data. Source is on GitHub.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Examples
Four more sites show what a Quarto site can grow into.

Chad Hazlett, a professor at UCLA, adds a publications page and a software page to the three pages you will build. Source is on GitHub.
Christopher Kenny, a postdoc at Princeton, adds software, a blog, and a page for the Quarto extensions he writes. Source is on GitHub.
Frederick Solt, a professor at Iowa, has about 180 pages: a blog, software, and a site for each of his data projects. Source is on GitHub.
Rob Hyndman, a professor of statistics at Monash, has nearly 900 pages: a blog, publications, software, seminars, and teaching. Source is on GitHub, though he hosts the site on his own server.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Before the workshop
Here’s what you should do before the workshop. Most of you should already have most of these.

A GitHub account. Sign up free at github.com/signup. Choose the username carefully, because it becomes your web address. johnasmith gives the site johnasmith.github.io. Use your name, all lowercase, nothing tied to FSU, and no gamer tags. Happy Git with R has good advice on picking one. If your existing username would look odd on a CV, change it before the workshop.
GitHub Desktop. Install from desktop.github.com. Make sure to get signed in to your account (GitHub Desktop → Settings → Accounts on a Mac, File → Options → Accounts on Windows).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Before the workshop

R and RStudio. Install the latest version from posit.co. Any version since 2025 or so works, too. Quarto comes built into RStudio. Check RStudio → About RStudio if you aren’t sure.
A professional headshot, cropped square.
Your CV as a PDF.
An ORCID iD. Register for free at orcid.org/register.
Your Google Scholar profile URL. Only if you have a profile. No profile yet is fine.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
How this works

We write our pages as plain text files.
We use Quarto to turn them into a website in a folder called docs/, which makes GitHub Pages simple.
We use GitHub Desktop to send that folder to GitHub (and GitHub Pages serves it to the world).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Make the project in RStudio
Done by 2:15.
In RStudio, click File → New Project… → New Directory → Quarto Website. Fill in the pane that follows.

Directory name: USERNAME.github.io, all lowercase. This exact name puts your site at https://USERNAME.github.io. If you use any other name, your site will be at USERNAME.github.io/that-other-name/.
Create project as subdirectory of: somewhere you will find it again. I keep my website in Dropbox/, but git and Dropbox don’t always play nicely.
Engine: leave it as it is.
Check Create a git repository. You’ll need the git repo for GitHub Desktop later.
Leave Use renv with this project unchecked.

Click Create Project. RStudio reopens with your new project loaded.

section: Add your photo and your CV
text:
Add your photo and your CV
Done by 2:55.
Your headshot and your CV are files rather than text. Find them in Finder (on a Mac) or File Explorer (on Windows). Right-click and copy these files (together or one at a time). In RStudio, go to the Files pane and choose More → Show Folder in New Window. You’ll see your project folder open in a new window, with _quarto.yml and your .qmd files already in it.
Paste both files in. Rename them exactly:

title: Build Your First Academic Website
section: Add your photo and your CV
text:
Add your photo and your CV






Any PDF works the same way


A working paper, a syllabus, and conference slides would work the same way. Drop the file into the project folder, link it from any page (e.g., [PDF](smith-turnout-2026.pdf) on your research page), and render. Quarto copies every file your pages link to into docs/, so the link will work on the live site with no upload step.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Add a .nojekyll file
Click into the Console at the bottom left and run:
file.create(".nojekyll")
It prints TRUE and creates an empty file.
Without this strange file, GitHub Pages will run your folder through a blog engine called Jekyll. We don’t want to do that because we’re rendering locally. The empty .nojekyll file turns that off. Quarto’s documentation recommends this.

Fix anything broken.

Click File → Add local repository…, click Choose…, and select your USERNAME.github.io folder. Then click Add repository.

Turn on GitHub Pages
Live by 3:30.
On github.com, open your new repository and update the settings:

Click Settings at the top, then Pages down the left side.
Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Updating your site
To update your site:

Edit the .qmd file in RStudio. Save it.
Click Build → Render Website.
In GitHub Desktop, write a short summary, click Commit to main, then click Push origin.

These updates will appear on your live site about two minutes later (but can take longer).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Extension: your own web address
USERNAME.github.io is free and perfectly reasonable. A custom domain like johnasmith.com costs about $15 a year and looks a little more polished.
Choosing the name. Your name makes the best address.

johnasmith.com is the best.
jasmith.com, johnsmith.io, and jsmith.co are good also.
Skip hyphens, digits, and anything that ties you to a place or a field. johnsmithfsupolitical.science is a poor choice.

Try names in Domainr. It checks many related domain names at once and shows which ones are available. (But don’t buy it from Domainr.)

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Extension: your own web address
Buying it. Search for the name on Namecheap, add it to the cart, and check out. A .com domain name costs about $10 the first year and about $15 a year after that. Accept the free WHOIS protection; decline the other add-ons.
Connecting it.

On Namecheap, click Domain List → Manage → Advanced DNS.

Delete any records already in the list. A new domain might have a www CNAME pointing at Namecheap’s parking page and a URL Redirect on @. Remove these; both conflict with the records below.
Add nine records. Namecheap’s own GitHub Pages guide describes the first five. The four AAAA records point the bare domain at GitHub over IPv6.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
Extension: your own web address

In the RStudio console, run writeLines("johnasmith.com", "CNAME") (replace your own domain in the quotes). This creates a file named CNAME that has just the domain. Quarto copies it into docs/ on every render, which is how GitHub knows the domain belongs to this site. Render, commit, push.
In your repository on github.com, click Settings → Pages, type johnasmith.com into Custom domain, and click Save. GitHub checks your DNS records, which usually takes minutes but can take up to a day. When the check passes, check Enforce HTTPS. GitHub documentation says the box can take up to a day to become clickable. Once you check it, the certificate usually arrives within a few minutes. If it doesn’t, remove the custom domain, add it again, and click Save. (If GitHub Desktop offers Pull origin afterward, click it; GitHub sometimes adds a small commit of its own when you save the domain.)

Your site is now live at the new address; the old USERNAME.github.io address keeps working as well.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
How I made this guide



I built this guide with a lot of help from Claude Code. I walked Claude Code through how I recommend using Quarto to build an academic website, and we built a simple website together. Then Claude Code helped me draft the step-by-step instructions, then rewrite and verify them.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
1 What you’ll build
Follow this guide to build your first academic website:

a home page with your photo and a short bio
a research page
a teaching page
a link to your CV

Your website will be at https://USERNAME.github.io. There’s no payment required unless you want a custom domain name (see the extension at the end).
USERNAME is a placeholder for your own GitHub username. My USERNAME is carlislerainey, so my repository is called carlislerainey.github.io and my site is at https://carlislerainey.github.io. Put your USERNAME wherever you see the placeholder.



The home page you are about to build.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
2 Examples
Have a look at the sites below. These are made using a process similar to the one described in this guide.
These three are pretty close to what you’ll have after you finish this guide:

Artur Baranov, a PhD candidate at Northwestern, uses jolla, the centered layout we start from. Source is on GitHub.
Maranda Joyce, a PhD candidate at Rice, uses trestles and one of Quarto’s dark themes. Source is on GitHub.
Tyler Rongxuan Chen, a PhD candidate at Michigan, uses solana and almost the same row of buttons you will make. Source is on GitHub.

These two have a bit of customization.

Charlotte Kuberka, a PhD candidate at LSE, kept trestles and restyled it to match her CV. Source is on GitHub.
Frederik Hjorth, a professor at Copenhagen, has a page each for his papers, his teaching, and his data. Source is on GitHub.

Four more sites show what a Quarto site can grow into.

Chad Hazlett, a professor at UCLA, adds a publications page and a software page to the three pages you will build. Source is on GitHub.
Christopher Kenny, a postdoc at Princeton, adds software, a blog, and a page for the Quarto extensions he writes. Source is on GitHub.
Frederick Solt, a professor at Iowa, has about 180 pages: a blog, software, and a site for each of his data projects. Source is on GitHub.
Rob Hyndman, a professor of statistics at Monash, has nearly 900 pages: a blog, publications, software, seminars, and teaching. Source is on GitHub, though he hosts the site on his own server.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
3 Before the workshop
Here’s what you should do before the workshop. Most of you should already have most of these.

A GitHub account. Sign up free at github.com/signup. Choose the username carefully, because it becomes your web address. johnasmith gives the site johnasmith.github.io. Use your name, all lowercase, nothing tied to FSU, and no gamer tags. Happy Git with R has good advice on picking one. If your existing username would look odd on a CV, change it before the workshop.
GitHub Desktop. Install from desktop.github.com. Make sure to get signed in to your account (GitHub Desktop → Settings → Accounts on a Mac, File → Options → Accounts on Windows).
R and RStudio. Install the latest version from posit.co. Any version since 2025 or so works, too. Quarto comes built into RStudio. Check RStudio → About RStudio if you aren’t sure.
A professional headshot, cropped square.
Your CV as a PDF.
An ORCID iD. Register for free at orcid.org/register.
Your Google Scholar profile URL. Only if you have a profile. No profile yet is fine.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
4 How this works

We write our pages as plain text files.
We use Quarto to turn them into a website in a folder called docs/, which makes GitHub Pages simple.
We use GitHub Desktop to send that folder to GitHub (and GitHub Pages serves it to the world).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
5 Make the project in RStudio
Done by 2:15.
In RStudio, click File → New Project… → New Directory → Quarto Website. Fill in the pane that follows.

Directory name: USERNAME.github.io, all lowercase. This exact name puts your site at https://USERNAME.github.io. If you use any other name, your site will be at USERNAME.github.io/that-other-name/.
Create project as subdirectory of: somewhere you will find it again. I keep my website in Dropbox/, but git and Dropbox don’t always play nicely.
Engine: leave it as it is.
Check Create a git repository. You’ll need the git repo for GitHub Desktop later.
Leave Use renv with this project unchecked.

Click Create Project. RStudio reopens with your new project loaded.

6 Render the site Quarto gave you
Done by 2:20.
Quarto has already added a working website. Before we change anything, look at what it added.
In the Files pane (bottom right) you will find four files:







File
What it is




_quarto.yml
The settings for your whole site: title, navigation bar, theme.

Your home page.


about.qmd

The Build tab’s Render Website button.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
section: 7 Point your site at the docs folder
text:
7 Point your site at the docs folder
Done by 2:30.
Open _quarto.yml from the Files pane, select everything in it, delete it, and replace it with this:
# The whole site is configured in this one file. The pages are the .qmd files
# next to it; the rendered site goes in docs/.
# Everything this file accepts: https://quarto.org/docs/reference/projects/websites.html

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs        # GitHub Pages can serve a site straight from docs/.

website:
  title: "Your Name"      # Shown at the left end of the navbar and in the browser tab.
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: Home
        href: index.qmd
      - research.qmd      # Link text comes from the page's own title.
      - teaching.qmd
      - text: CV
        href: cv.pdf      # The CV is a PDF, not a page. Replace the file; keep the name.
  # Three additions you will probably want, in the order people usually want them:
  #   - Another page (talks, software, data). Create talks.qmd with a title: line at
  #     the top, then add "- talks.qmd" to the navbar list above. A blog is one step
  #     more, a page that lists posts: https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-blog.html
  #   - Link previews. When someone shares your site on Bluesky or in Slack, show a
  #     card with your name and photo instead of a bare URL: add
  #     "site-url: https://USERNAME.github.io" and "open-graph: true" at this indent.
  #     (site-url also gives search engines a sitemap.)
  #   - Visitor counts, if you want them: create a free Google Analytics property,
  #     then add its ID here as google-analytics: "G-XXXXXXXXXX", at this indent.
  # More additions like these: https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-tools.html

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo          # Quarto's default look. Try flatly (dark navbar), litera (serif
                          # text), or sandstone. Change the word, re-render. All 25 themes,
                          # with pictures: https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html
    css: styles.css       # Extra styling on top of the theme. The file is empty; your own
                          # CSS rules go there if a theme setting ever isn't enough.
We changed five things away from the Quarto default:

output-dir: docs sends the finished site to docs/ instead of _site/. GitHub Pages will serve a folder named docs (but not one called _site/).
title: is your name.
The navbar lists Research, Teaching, and your CV instead of the example “about” page.
theme: cosmo replaces a two-item list. The brand entry it came with uses a _brand.yml file of custom colors and fonts, which you don’t have.
toc: true is deleted, because a table of contents on a webpage is usually clutter.

css: styles.css stays. The file is empty and we won’t add anything today. Your own CSS rules can go there later.






Warning



YAML is particular about spaces. The spaces create the indentation that gives the file its structure. Keep the spaces exactly as they appear above. Use spaces rather than tabs.


Delete the _site folder you made a moment ago. Check the box beside it in the Files pane and click Delete. We won’t need it again.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
8 Build your three pages
Done by 2:50.
Start by deleting the example page we don’t need. Check about.qmd in the Files pane, then click Delete.
Your home page. Open index.qmd, select everything, and replace it with Quarto syntax below. Put in your own name, bio, email address, Scholar URL, and ORCID iD:
---
title: "Your Name"
image: headshot.jpg          # Your photo. Square images look best. Replace the file; keep the name.
image-alt: "Your Name"       # What a screen reader says for the photo. Use your name here too.
about:
  template: jolla            # Centered: photo, name, bio, buttons. Three things to try:
                             #   - template: trestles   (photo on the left, bio on the right)
                             #   - template: solana     (bio on the left, photo on the right)
                             #   - image-shape: rectangle   (or rounded; on its own line at this indent)
                             # All home-page options, with pictures:
                             # https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-about.html
  links:                     # The buttons under the bio. Try adding github, linkedin,
    - icon: envelope         # or twitter-x. Every icon name: https://icons.getbootstrap.com/
      text: Email
      href: mailto:you@fsu.edu
    - icon: file-earmark-pdf
      text: CV
      href: cv.pdf
    - icon: google
      text: Google Scholar
      href: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XXXXXXXXXXXX
    - icon: person-vcard     # There is no ORCID icon in the set; use an ID card.
      text: ORCID
      href: https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000
---

<!-- Everything below the front matter is the bio. Keep this short; two or three short paragraphs
     is plenty. Say who you are, what you study, and what you teach. Maybe add one sentence on your dissertation. -->

I am a Ph.D. student in the Department of Political Science at Florida State University. I study American politics and political behavior, with a focus on how citizens form and change their opinions. I teach courses on American and comparative politics. My dissertation, "Title of the Dissertation," asks how a question of interest shapes an outcome of interest.

Before starting my Ph.D. at FSU, I earned a B.A. in political science from Institution in 2022.
If you don’t have a Google Scholar profile yet, delete its three lines. Google Scholar is only important once you accumulate citations.
    - icon: google
      text: Google Scholar
      href: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XXXXXXXXXXXX
To add another button (e.g., GitHub, LinkedIn), copy the three-line pattern and pick an icon name.
Your research page. Click File → New File → Text File, paste the block below, then choose File → Save As… and name it exactly research.qmd:
---

title: Build Your First Academic Website
section: 9 Add your photo and your CV
text:
9 Add your photo and your CV
Done by 2:55.
Your headshot and your CV are files rather than text. Find them in Finder (on a Mac) or File Explorer (on Windows). Right-click and copy these files (together or one at a time). In RStudio, go to the Files pane and choose More → Show Folder in New Window. You’ll see your project folder open in a new window, with _quarto.yml and your .qmd files already in it.
Paste both files in. Rename them exactly:

headshot.jpg
cv.pdf







Any PDF works the same way



A working paper, a syllabus, and conference slides would work the same way. Drop the file into the project folder, link it from any page (e.g., [PDF](smith-turnout-2026.pdf) on your research page), and render. Quarto copies every file your pages link to into docs/, so the link will work on the live site with no upload step.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
10 Add a .nojekyll file
Click into the Console at the bottom left and run:
file.create(".nojekyll")
It prints TRUE and creates an empty file.
Without this strange file, GitHub Pages will run your folder through a blog engine called Jekyll. We don’t want to do that because we’re rendering locally. The empty .nojekyll file turns that off. Quarto’s documentation recommends this.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
section: 11 Check your site before you publish
text:
11 Check your site before you publish
Done by 3:00.
Go to Build → Render Website once more.
Then click the arrow at the top of the Viewer pane to open your site in a real browser. Before we publish it to GitHub, click through everything in the navigation bar:

Home shows your photo, your bio, and four working buttons.
Research and Teaching show your own content.
CV opens your PDF.

Fix anything broken.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
12 Rearrange your home page
Done by 3:05.
Quarto has five layout templates that you can use for your homepage (i.e., index.qmd). You can change it with the template: option.







Layout
Arrangement




jolla
Photo at the top, centered, with your name, bio, and buttons below it.


trestles
Photo and buttons in a left column, bio on the right.


solana
Name, buttons, and bio on the left, photo on the right.


marquee
One large image across the top, everything else stacked below.


broadside
Photo on the left, name, bio, and buttons on the right.




Open index.qmd and change template: jolla to template: trestles. Save, then click Render Website. Look for the changes.
Try template: solana next.
Keep the one you like. The screenshots in the rest of this guide use jolla.










trestles: photo on the left.







solana: photo on the right.





marquee uses a wide banner image, not a square headshot. Pictures of all five layouts are in the Quarto documentation.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
13 Pick a theme
Done by 3:10.
You can change the overall look of your site with the theme: option. Quarto has 25 themes you can choose from.

Open _quarto.yml and change theme: cosmo to theme: flatly. Save and render. Notice the change.
Try sandstone, litera, and zephyr. All four are professional choices appropriate for an academic site, so pick whichever you like. You can see full-size previews of all 25 at bootswatch.com.










flatly: dark navbar.







sandstone: warm and muted.









litera: serif body text.







zephyr: rounded and airy.






Just for fun, try sketchy and/or vapor. (Then change back to your favorite.)










sketchy.







vapor.

section: 14 Publish your site with GitHub Desktop
text:
14 Publish your site with GitHub Desktop
Done by 3:20.
Open GitHub Desktop.

Click File → Add local repository…, click Choose…, and select your USERNAME.github.io folder. Then click Add repository.
Your files will be listed under the Changes tab. There will be a lot of them. You need them all, so leave everything checked.
At the bottom left, type Initial commit in the Summary box. Then click Commit to main. (Your button may say master instead; remember which one it says.)
At the top of the window, click Publish repository.




The Changes tab before the first commit.








Important



Uncheck Keep this code private before you publish. With a free account, GitHub Pages only works for public repositories.





The Publish dialog, with the private box unchecked.


Click Publish repository. Your new repository will appear on github.com in a few seconds.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
15 Turn on GitHub Pages
Live by 3:30.
On github.com, open your new repository and update the settings:

Click Settings at the top, then Pages down the left side.
Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.
Set Branch to main (or to master if that is what your commit button said) and set the folder beside it to /docs. Click Save.
Wait about two minutes, then visit https://USERNAME.github.io. GitHub documentation says this can take up to ten minutes.




The Pages settings, pointed at the docs folder.

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
16 Updating your site
To update your site:

Edit the .qmd file in RStudio. Save it.
Click Build → Render Website.
In GitHub Desktop, write a short summary, click Commit to main, then click Push origin.

These updates will appear on your live site about two minutes later (but can take longer).

title: Build Your First Academic Website
text:
17 Extension: your own web address
USERNAME.github.io is free and perfectly reasonable. A custom domain like johnasmith.com costs about $15 a year and looks a little more polished.
Choosing the name. Your name makes the best address.

johnasmith.com is the best.
jasmith.com, johnsmith.io, and jsmith.co are good also.
Skip hyphens, digits, and anything that ties you to a place or a field. johnsmithfsupolitical.science is a poor choice.

Try names in Domainr. It checks many related domain names at once and shows which ones are available. (But don’t buy it from Domainr.)
Buying it. Search for the name on Namecheap, add it to the cart, and check out. A .com domain name costs about $10 the first year and about $15 a year after that. Accept the free WHOIS protection; decline the other add-ons.
Connecting it.

On Namecheap, click Domain List → Manage → Advanced DNS.

Delete any records already in the list. A new domain might have a www CNAME pointing at Namecheap’s parking page and a URL Redirect on @. Remove these; both conflict with the records below.
Add nine records. Namecheap’s own GitHub Pages guide describes the first five. The four AAAA records point the bare domain at GitHub over IPv6.

In the RStudio console, run writeLines("johnasmith.com", "CNAME") (replace your own domain in the quotes). This creates a file named CNAME that has just the domain. Quarto copies it into docs/ on every render, which is how GitHub knows the domain belongs to this site. Render, commit, push.
In your repository on github.com, click Settings → Pages, type johnasmith.com into Custom domain, and click Save. GitHub checks your DNS records, which usually takes minutes but can take up to a day. When the check passes, check Enforce HTTPS. GitHub documentation says the box can take up to a day to become clickable. Once you check it, the certificate usually arrives within a few minutes. If it doesn’t, remove the custom domain, add it again, and click Save. (If GitHub Desktop offers Pull origin afterward, click it; GitHub sometimes adds a small commit of its own when you save the domain.)

Your site is now live at the new address; the old USERNAME.github.io address keeps working as well.
